context: The array nums has five slots indexed from 0 to 4. It initially stores [1, 2, 5, 4, 0], but only the first four elements, [1, 2, 5, 4], are valid. The 0 at index 4 is a placeholder. The goal is to insert 3 at index 1 while preserving the relative order of the existing valid elements.
prose.result: After insertion, all five slots hold valid elements, so the caller updates the logical length to 5. The example insert function only assigns values to slots. When the text says a fixed-length array “loses” its last element, what is overwritten here is the placeholder 0. All four original valid elements survive. If all five slots were already in use, the last valid element would be lost, so the array would need to grow first or the insertion would have to be rejected.

steps.announcement: The initial array is [1, 2, 5, 4, 0]. The existing elements will shift right before 3 is inserted at index 1.
steps.explanation: The array stores [1, 2, 5, 4, 0], with logical length 4 and a trailing placeholder 0. Writing 3 directly at index 1 would overwrite the valid element 2, so first copy the elements at indices 1 through 3 one place to the right.
steps.key_state: Prepare to insert 3 at index 1. The array stores [1, 2, 5, 4, 0], the valid sequence is [1, 2, 5, 4], and the trailing 0 is a placeholder.

steps.announcement: Execute nums[4] = nums[3] to copy the 4 at index 3 to index 4, overwriting the placeholder 0.

steps.key_state: After nums[4] = nums[3] copies 4, the array stores [1, 2, 5, 4, 4].
steps.title: Copy the last valid element, 4

steps.announcement: Execute nums[3] = nums[2] to copy the 5 at index 2 to index 3.
steps.explanation: Execute nums[3] = nums[2] to copy 5 to index 3. The array now stores [1, 2, 5, 5, 4]. The original 4 is safe in the last slot. Next, copy 2 and then write 3. The recorded logical length is still 4.
steps.key_state: After nums[3] = nums[2] copies 5, the array stores [1, 2, 5, 5, 4]. Only 4 and 5 have been copied. The 3 has not been written yet.
steps.title: Copy 5

steps.announcement: Execute nums[2] = nums[1] to copy the 2 at index 1 to index 2. Index 1 can now be overwritten safely.
steps.explanation: Execute nums[2] = nums[1] to copy 2 to index 2. The array now stores [1, 2, 2, 5, 4]. The original 2, 5, and 4 have shifted right. Index 1 still holds 2 but can safely be overwritten. The 3 has not been written yet, and the recorded logical length is still 4.
steps.key_state: After nums[2] = nums[1] copies 2, the shift is complete. The array stores [1, 2, 2, 5, 4] and is ready for 3.
steps.title: Copy 2

steps.announcement: Writing 3 at index 1 completes the insertion. The array is [1, 3, 2, 5, 4], and the caller updates the logical length to 5.
steps.explanation: Execute nums[1] = 3. The array now stores [1, 3, 2, 5, 4]. Writing the new element completes the insertion. The number of valid elements increases from 4 to 5, and the caller updates the logical length.
steps.key_state: After nums[1] = 3, the final contents are [1, 3, 2, 5, 4]. The caller updates the logical length to 5.
steps.title: Write 3

frames.explanation: Copying from the end back toward the insertion point saves each needed element in the slot to its right before overwriting it. Copying leaves the source slot intact, so duplicate values appear temporarily. Inserting in the middle of an array moves O(n) elements on average.
